title: KV sharded page-scheduling and OOM mitigation proposal for blocked/paged cache
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description:
Goal:
Design and prototype a sharded, page-oriented KV cache scheduler that cooperates with continuous batching to avoid GPU OOMs while retaining low tail latency. This ticket captures the implementation approach, API/ABI constraints, test plan, rollout strategy, and acceptance criteria.

Background / motivation:
- Current blocked/paged KV cache implementations reduce peak GPU memory but create head-of-line blocking when hot attention keys are paged in synchronously.
- Continuous batching increases request parallelism and can amplify hot-key contention; naive prefetch strategies either overfetch (wasting memory) or underfetch (causing stalls).
- We need an approach that trades a small increase in average memory residency for significantly fewer stalls and predictable SLOs.

Design principles:
1) Sharded page ownership: split KV space by shard IDs (model layer + token-range) and assign each shard to a logical owner thread on the host. This keeps page metadata and eviction decisions local and lock-light.
2) Page granularity: use 1MiB logical pages composed of fixed-size blocks (e.g., 64KiB blocks) to allow sub-page reuse accounting while keeping DMA-friendly IO sizes.
3) Hotness-driven scheduling: maintain an LRU+frequency estimator per shard; schedule GPU page residency based on a combined score: hotness * request_affinity_weight + prefetch_bonus.
4) Batch-aware prefetching: prefetch pages for the active batch window only; continuous batching provides visibility of upcoming seq lengths and request pinning, so the scheduler boosts pages referenced by pending batches.
5) Staged async transfer: use pinned host staging buffers + CUDA async copies with stream per-shard to overlap transfer with kernel dispatch; degrade gracefully to prioritized synchronous migrations only if transfer latency exceeds a threshold.
6) Memory reservation windows: allow the serving runtime to reserve a small adjustable pool on GPU for prefetch budget per shard to avoid global OOMs. Global admission control rejects or routes requests to cheaper model variants when reservation budget is exhausted.

Data structures & metadata layout:
- PageTableEntry (PTE) per logical page (flattened arrays): state enum {ResidentGPU, InTransit, ResidentHost, Evicted}, last_access_ts, access_count, owner_shard, pinned_count. PTEs are stored in host memory (NUMA-aware) and exposed read-only to inference threads.
- ShardScheduler: per-shard min-heap keyed by score; small working set list for resident pages.
- TransferQueue: per-shard ring buffers for pending async transfers; items include page_id, transfer_type, priority, batch_id_affinity.

Algorithms (high level):
- On request arrival: read page ids referenced by KV lookup; consult PTEs. If ResidentGPU -> fine. If InTransit -> attach request to transfer completion future. If ResidentHost/Evicted -> escalate to ShardScheduler to consider prefetch.
- Scheduling step (triggered by batching window close or timeout): compute scores for pages touched by pending batches. For top-N pages per shard, issue async transfer if budget allows. If budget exhausted, attempt to pick lower-cost candidate in another shard (cross-shard cooperation) or signal admission controller to degrade incoming request.
- Eviction policy: hybrid CLOCK-ApproxLFU where resident pages are given a second-chance via pinned_count and recent_batch_affinity. When evicting, prefer blocks within the least-recently-used page and writeback only if modified (we are read-only KV so writebacks are rare).

OOM mitigation and graceful fallback:
- Soft budgets: the runtime enforces a soft cap; when observed GPU memory approaches hard limit, background evictor accelerates eviction and shrinks prefetch budgets.
- Priority-based admission: requests tagged low-priority (e.g., background embedding recompute) are preemptively routed to CPU fallback or cheaper quantized model.
- Incremental backoff: when a transfer cannot complete within the batch latency budget, mark the offending page as "unstable" and lower its prefetch weight for some cooling period. This prevents thrash loops.

Integration with continuous batching:
- The batching layer annotates batches with predicted page footprint (histogram of page IDs) aggregated from past N similar requests. This feeds the shard scheduler to make pro-active transfer decisions.
- For streaming responses, the scheduler focuses first on immediate decode KV pages and delays long-tail pages referenced only by later decoding steps.

Metrics and observability (what we will track):
- Page residency ratio (GPU/host) per shard
- Async transfer latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99)
- Stall counts and stall latency added to request tail
- OOM events and graceful fallback counts
- Prefetch hit rate and wasted prefetch memory (bytes fetched but not used within window)

Testing & validation plan:
1) Unit tests for PTE state transitions and ShardScheduler scoring function.
2) Microbench cluster test with synthetic hot-key skew traces to validate stall reduction vs. baseline.
3) Integration test with continuous batcher replaying production traffic (sample from production trace) to measure p95/p99 latency improvements and prefetch waste.
4) Fault injection: inject prolonged transfer latencies and verify graceful fallbacks and cooling heuristics.

Rollout strategy:
- Stage 1 (canary): run scheduler as opt-in flag for 5% of dedicated customers with heavy KV workload. Collect metrics and compare to baseline for 7 days.
- Stage 2 (gradual): increase to 25% after tuning budgets and default weights. Enable more aggressive prefetch only for customers with permissive budgets.
- Stage 3 (default): enable widely with conservative budgets and expose knobs in console for prefetch budget per tenant.

Acceptance criteria:
- p99 token-level stall latency reduced by >= 40% on high-skew workloads vs current blocked-paging baseline.
- Overall GPU memory utilization increased by <= 10% (acceptable tradeoff).
- No increase in production OOM rate; any OOMs must be explainable and covered by fallback routes.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Page size: 1MiB chosen for DMA efficiency, but smaller pages reduce wasted fetch — need empirical sweep.
- Cross-shard cooperation cost: beneficial for global fairness but adds communication overhead. Start with occasional cross-shard leases.
- Heuristic cold-starts: for new models with no access history, warm-up strategy required (sample-based prefetch).

Implementation notes / timeline:
- Week 1: implement PTE and ShardScheduler skeleton + unit tests (ENG-33413 follow-up for test harness).
- Week 2: async transfer plumbing, pinned buffers, CUDA stream-per-shard prototype.
- Week 3: integrate with continuous batcher annotations and end-to-end microbench.
- Week 4: canary rollout and metrics dashboard.
